# The studies we depend on, reproduced

*Companion to [Questions we need Emily to answer](/writing/questions-for-emily-testing-a-theory-of-the-interface) and [the essay](/writing/testing-a-theory-of-the-interface-with-an-ontology). Generated by `scripts/reproduce_studies.py`.*

Each page takes one paper we depend on, writes its sample and process history in our language as the paper states them, simulates it, and sets the result beside the paper's numbers. The sample and history were re-read from each PDF by a second agent that had not seen our transcriptions, and every item is marked: same, approximated, assumed, differs, or not in ours. Nothing was fitted for these pages; every model runs with the parameters recorded when it was last scored. No value has been checked by a person, which is what these pages are for.

**Two different grades.** *Reproducible from the paper?* grades the paper as a source: whether it states its sample, every step and every step's timing well enough that a simulation needs no choices of ours. It changes only when more is learned about the experiment. *How well our simulation matches* grades us: the share of the paper's numbers our simulation lands within tolerance of (High: three quarters or more; Moderate: two fifths or more; Low: fewer), with the median error, what the alignment adds on samples held out of it, and the first score recorded for the study. This is the column that moves as the language and the programs improve.

## How to read a page

- **The player** shows the sample in three dimensions with its history on a clock. Layer thicknesses and read-outs are the simulation's values at that moment.
- **The match diagram** puts the paper's words on the left and what we simulate on the right, one row per sample property and per step.
- **Their terms and ours** maps the paper's vocabulary onto the language and the ontology.
- **The simulation in our language** is the complete input, and the model program as written.
- **The difference chart** shows, for each number the paper reports, how far our simulation is from it.

## What the second reading found, across all studies

- **Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990.** Every wafer was pulled in under 5 s in the oxidizing gas. The recipe stored with each measurement stops at the end of the oxidation (plus the anneal); the pull is on the source record, not in the history. Written as a step it moves the simulated fixed charge of the (100), 1000 °C, 1 h wafer from 1.46 to 1.58 × 10^11 cm^-2.
- **Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990.** The report describes two sample sets. Dry oxygen under 6 ppm water, the HF-last clean and boron doping are stated for the non-cleanroom set only; for the cleanroom set, which all our electrical values come from, the gas is never named. Our library records one set of conditions for the source.
- **Deal, Sklar, Grove and Snow 1967.** The recipe stored with each of these measurements is one step: the pull, or the anneal. The oxidation that came before it (1200 °C, 60 min, dry oxygen, 0.2 µm) is absent, and so is the pull that must follow an anneal.
- **Deal, Sklar, Grove and Snow 1967.** The argon anneal at 920 °C is stored as `inert_N2`. The language has had `inert_Ar` since the SiC work; the row was never updated.
- **Deal and Razouk 1980.** The stored recipes begin after the oxidation. Written out in full, each history is the oxidation (300, 84 or 28 min), the anneal if any, the pull, and ten minutes at 400 °C after metallization.
- **Deal and Razouk 1980.** The argon runs (TR-4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24) are stored as nitrogen anneals. The paper treats the two gases as one curve, so the numbers are not affected; the record is wrong.
- **Hung 1987.** The stored recipes have one or two RUNs: the oxidation and, in chapter 4 and the anneal series, the nitrogen anneal. The thesis's Appendix adds a 3 min boat-in in the oxidation gas, a 3 min boat-out in nitrogen (chapter 4), a fast pull in the oxidation gas (chapter 5), and in chapter 4 a 30 min forming-gas anneal with 15 min of nitrogen before and after. None of these is in the stored recipes.
- **Hung 1987.** The anneal series P (1050 °C, 20% O2) is stored with 27 min of oxidation, “inferred from the thickness”; Table 5.1b prints 20 min. The datasets were built before Table 5.1b was read.
- **Song, Dhar, Feldman, Chung and Williams 2004.** Our stored recipe (one hold in dry oxygen at the stated temperature) is what the paper states. The second reading found nothing our encoding contradicts.
- **Song, Dhar, Feldman, Chung and Williams 2004.** The paper never says whether the points on a curve are separate samples or one sample re-oxidized. Our simulation treats each time as an uninterrupted oxidation from a clean surface.
- **Kobayashi et al. 2017.** Oxidation and argon anneal were done in different furnaces, so each annealed sample was cooled, unloaded and reheated in between. Our stored history runs the anneal straight after the oxidation.
- **Kobayashi et al. 2017.** Five minutes of argon and forty minutes of oxidation at 1300 °C are our choices from the ranges the paper gives (1 to 10 min; 40 min or 1 h 20 min). The stored records present them as the recipe.
- **Goncharova et al. 2011.** The stored recipe gives the anneal as dry oxygen at one atmosphere. The paper's gas is 18O2 at 0.01 Torr, about 1.3 × 10^-5 atm. No program reads the pressure, so the numbers do not change, but the fitted rates belong to that pressure and cannot be carried to another.
- **Goncharova et al. 2011.** Our oxygen dataset labels the lowest temperature 773 K and our profile dataset labels the same anneal 763 K. The paper uses both, and 490 °C; the figures say 763 K.
- **Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982.** The stored recipes (data/derived/akinwande_1982_nf.csv through scripts/canonical_measurements.py) begin with the 2 s pull. The 60 min of argon pre-heat, HCl etch and purge and the 75 min oxidation are not steps; the oxidation enters the program only as a constant (T_ox = 1000 °C). For the charge this changes nothing, because the program starts from the steady value at the oxidation temperature.
- **Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982.** Every argon anneal is stored as AMBIENT inert_N2. The report says argon with under 1 ppm water. Both have no oxygen, so the numbers are the same; the record is wrong.
- **Razouk and Deal 1979.** There is no dataset in data/derived for this paper and no stored recipe: the project's analyses read figures_agent_read_UNVERIFIED.csv directly, with the oxidation times 360 and 60 min for Figure 7 only and no history for Figures 8 and 13.
- **Razouk and Deal 1979.** The two readings of the figures (ours earlier, and the second reading) agree within 5% on 41 of the 44 values both hold. They disagree on three: Figure 13 after hydrogen at 1200 °C (0.60 earlier, 0.52 in the second reading, 13%), Figure 7 (100) at 1200 °C, 10 min in nitrogen, unannealed (3.2 against 3.0, 6%) and the same in argon for 60 min after hydrogen (0.123 against 0.13, 6%). The values compared on this page are the earlier reading's, which the project's analyses use. The second reading also gives what the first did not: Figure 13 before hydrogen and after a 450 °C, 25% H2 anneal, and the fixed charge of Figures 7 and 9.
- **Deal and Grove 1965.** Our transcription of Table II (`tables_agent_read_UNVERIFIED.csv`) and the second reading agree in all 24 cells: none differs.
- **Deal and Grove 1965.** The program does not carry the paper's activation energies. It carries a least-squares Arrhenius line through the six Table II rows: E_B = 1.286 eV against the paper's 28.5 kcal/mole (1.236 eV), and E_BA = 2.030 eV against 46.0 kcal/mole (1.995 eV). At the table's own temperatures the line is off the table by up to 15% (B at 1200 °C, B/A at 800 °C); see the table below.
- **Krzeminski et al. 2007.** The stored recipe for the paper's own wafers is one RUN of 90 min at 725 or 750 °C in dry oxygen. The paper's cycle is a load at 675/700 °C, a 30 min ramp in 9% oxygen, the main stage in oxygen, 10 min of ramp-down and 30 min of reflow in nitrogen. The ramp is the one that matters: it grows 1.53 or 1.96 nm, all of the oxide at “0 min”.
- **Krzeminski et al. 2007.** The other-laboratory score in `evaluations/growth_search_report.json` (6 of 10, 13% low at 725 °C) started the law at the measured 1.53 or 1.96 nm. The predictor cannot do that: it starts every history at the fitted 1.71 nm. Run through the predictor with the stored recipe, the same points come out between 1% high and 14% low at 725 °C and 8 to 11% low at 750 °C, and the 0 min points (excluded from the search's score) 12% high and 13% low. The two scores of one program on one dataset differ because the starting oxide lives in different places.
- **Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023.** The stored recipe for every Si wire is one steam step of 779.5 s at 850 °C. That is the time the bulk slope of Figure A1 (1.46 nm/min) needs to grow 19 nm from zero; the paper's example time is 7.7 min (462 s). The difference, about 5.3 min, stands in for whatever oxide the bulk had before the steam: the ramp in oxygen, the 5 min hold, the native oxide. With 462 s of steam and nothing before it, the program gives the 94 nm wire 21.8 nm of oxide instead of the measured 33.4.
- **Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023.** The paper's furnace cycle has five simulated steps (nitrogen ramp, oxygen ramp, 5 min oxygen hold, steam, nitrogen cool-down); the stored recipe has one. The radial program grows nothing in the four we added, because its rate is proportional to p_H2O and it has no temperature dependence.
- **Krzeminski, Han and Larrieu 2012.** The stored recipe is one steam step of 600 or 1200 s at 850 °C. The paper states 850 °C, “wet” and the two times, and nothing else; the stored recipe adds pure steam at 1 atm. Our history adds an assumed ramp and an assumed oxide at time zero.
- **Krzeminski, Han and Larrieu 2012.** Every curve of Figure 1(a) starts at about 5 nm at t = 0. The radial program starts from bare silicon, so either the program misses 5 nm or the paper's times do not start at the start of oxidation. Writing that oxide as 90 s of steam before the stated time makes every wire thicker by 1 to 5 nm, which is the wrong direction for this paper.
- **Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005.** The stored LeGoues recipe is one step, 180 min of `wet_O2` at 800 °C. `wet_O2` carries no partial pressures, so the inventory program runs it as pure steam (p_H2O = 1). Written as the 55% steam that the paper's own C* implies, the inventory's enriched layer falls from 91 to 69 nm and the alloy consumed from 65 to 49 nm; the Rabie program's thickness does not change because it does not read the gas.
- **Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005.** The germanium-rich layer (50 nm, up to 75%) has no time in the paper. Our dataset row puts it at 180 min, the last point of Figure 4, and scores it as a value (75%) although the paper says “up to”.
- **David et al. 2015.** The dataset holds two rows of this paper (50% at 800 °C, 90 min; 50% at 750 °C, 6 h). The text supports the same 50% at 750, 850 and 900 °C too, but Figure 3b peaks near 45% at 900 °C, so the 900 °C row is the paper's sentence against its own figure.
- **David et al. 2015.** The stored recipe of the 6 h row is one 6 h hold. The paper's sample is a 34 nm film on 12 nm of silicon on oxide; by 6 h all the alloy is consumed. No stored field says so.
- **Wang, Hu and Irene 1994.** The stored recipe for each temperature is one hold in dry oxygen for the longest time. The paper's sequence has a heat-up in vacuum, a fill, the oxidation, an evacuation and a cooling in vacuum; written out, the heat-up and the cooling add about 0.04 nm in the program because it does not read the gas.
- **Wang, Hu and Irene 1994.** The starting oxide is a fitted parameter of the program (“starting oxide fixed” in the selected structure, a value fitted with the others). The paper's two figures disagree on it (about 0 nm in Figure 1a, about 1 nm in Figure 1b); the sample cannot carry it.

## What the language gained from reproducing these studies

Each addition below was forced by a paper that could not otherwise be written down as it was done. The words are in `ontology/isl_vocabulary.json` (`history_statements`) and the language reference, and the runtime refuses anything else.

| Added | Because | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `TIMING stated\|bound\|range\|assumed` on every step | Vitkavage's pull is “shorter than 5 sec”, Kobayashi's anneal “1 - 10 min”, and most loading and cooling is not stated at all. A history now says which of its numbers are the paper's. | `RUN Pull DURATION 5 TEMP 1000->400 AMBIENT dry_O2 TIMING bound` |
| `VARY <duration\|T_start\|T_end\|T_hold> <lo>..<hi>` | What a paper leaves open is an unknown with a range, not a number of ours. `scripts/align_study.py` searches these ranges against the paper's results, which turns alignment from a hand-written script into a query on the history. | `VARY duration 0.5..5 VARY T_end 300..800` |
| `PROFILE exponential TAU <s>` | A wafer leaving a furnace cools toward the room along a curve. A straight line to an assumed end temperature hid a model fault: the fixed-charge program keeps moving charge at low temperature. | `RUN Endcap DURATION 120 TEMP 400->25 AMBIENT dry_O2 PROFILE exponential TAU 30` |
| `EVENT <id> KIND <kind>` | Cleans, transfers between furnaces, storage, metallization and measurement were comments. Now they are statements in their place in the history, with a kind from the vocabulary. | `EVENT Transfer KIND transfer TIMING assumed` |
| Several `SAMPLE` blocks under one history | Vitkavage oxidized four orientations in one run, and their charge moves together from run to run. One history can now hold the wafers of a run. | `python -m isl_harness.predict run.isl` runs each wafer |
| Gas read by partial pressure | Writing the paper's own gas (dry oxygen with 6 ppm water; ¹⁸O₂ at 0.01 Torr; 20% oxygen in nitrogen) made programs written for `dry_O2` return nothing. | `AMBIENT mix:O2=0.999994,H2O=6.0e-6` |
| An orientation without constants is run on the (100) line, labelled outside scope | (110) and (511) had silently taken the (111) fixed-charge line and came out three to four times high. | |
| `STARTING_OXIDE_NM` on a sample, read by the growth programs | Every oxide started at the 1965 law's 23 nm (wet oxides included) or at a fitted 1.7 nm, whatever the wafer carried. Deal and Grove, Krzeminski 2007 and 2012, Müller and Goncharova each state a different starting oxide. | `SAMPLE W { FAMILY: Si_Planar; STARTING_OXIDE_NM: 1.0 }` |
| The thin-oxide and germanium growth programs read the oxygen pressure | They grew oxide in nitrogen and vacuum, and grew a 9% oxygen ramp as if it were pure oxygen (Hung 1987, Krzeminski 2007, Razouk and Deal 1979). The fits were made at 1 atm, so the fitted values stand. | |
| The fixed-charge program's exchange with oxygen stops as the wafer cools (`T_freeze`, a stated hypothesis) | Its oxygen rate, fitted at an activation energy of 0.05 eV, kept moving charge at room temperature: a realistic cool made Stanford's charge 3 to 5 times too high. Every history it was fitted on ended at 400 °C, so the cut-off was there all along, unstated. | cooling to 25 °C: 1.40 → 1.83 instead of → 6.4 × 10¹¹ cm⁻² |
| The alignment counts a refused history as a failure, keeps the paper's value when the data do not choose, and never sets an unknown no chosen sample carries | Reported by the agents aligning Hung, Kobayashi and Müller: refused rows had scored as perfect, and flat scans moved unknowns arbitrarily. | |

## What our language and ontology still cannot say

Collected from every page. Each is something a paper states, or a simulation needs, that cannot yet be written down; each says what it would change. This is the agenda for the next changes to the language.

- **Done 10 November: a furnace run shared by several samples.** A history may now hold several SAMPLE blocks under one CONTROL_TRAJECTORY, and `scripts/align_study.py` can share an unknown per run (`share = "run"`). Still missing: a record in the ontology that measurements came from one run. Before: The result above depends on four wafers having one history. A history file has one SAMPLE; the ontology has no record that measurements came from one run. A `BATCH` of samples under one `CONTROL_TRAJECTORY` would let one unknown be declared once and inferred from all of them. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **Done 10 November: an unknown with a range, as a statement.** `TIMING bound` and `VARY duration 0.5..5` now exist and drive the alignment search. Before: “Shorter than 5 sec” had to become `DURATION 5`. The language needs `DURATION 0.5..5` (a bound), and a status on each step's timing (stated, bound, assumed), which on this page is hand-written in Python. Then a scan like this one is a query, not a script. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **Partly done 10 November: cooling as a law.** `PROFILE exponential TAU` now exists; the charge program still needs a rate that freezes as the wafer cools. Before: A RUN's temperature is linear from start to end. A wafer leaving a furnace cools toward the room with a time constant. Without that, the end temperature of a pull (400 °C) is a cut-off that stands in for physics, and the charge program, whose oxygen rate barely depends on temperature (0.05 eV), keeps moving charge at 100 °C if a cooling step is written. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **Done 10 November: steps with no duration.** `EVENT <id> KIND <kind>` now records them in place. Still missing: an ontology class a program could read. Before: Clean, load, storage, metallization and measurement are comments in the history. The ontology has no classes for them that a program could read; an `EVENT` statement with a kind from the vocabulary would at least make them queryable. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **Sample properties a program can read.** Doping, wafer size, starting oxide and sample set are recorded and read by nothing. The starting oxide in particular is a parameter inside the growth program (23 nm) when it is a property of the wafer. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **Done 10 November: an orientation with no constants.** It now runs on the (100) line and is labelled outside the tested scope. Before: (110) and (511) fell back to (111) for fixed charge with a note; the number looked like any other. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **Partly done 10 November: gas by pressure, not by name.** The predictor now reads a gas by its partial pressures. Still open: the thin-oxide program grows oxide in nitrogen because it does not read the oxygen pressure. Before: Writing the stated moisture (`mix:O2=0.999994,H2O=6.0e-6`) made the fixed-charge program return nothing, because the predictor looks for the name `dry_O2`. And the thin-oxide program keeps growing oxide during a nitrogen step: it does not read the oxygen pressure. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **What a measurement is.** Fixed charge after a hydrogen anneal, apparent charge without one, and Deal's 1967 charge after 550 °C in nitrogen are three observables in the papers and one in ours. The work-function value behind every fixed charge here is not stated; an observation model for the C-V extraction would carry that assumption. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- **Repeatability as data.** The report's run-to-run scatter (up to 33%) is larger than the 10% we score against. A dataset should carry its own repeatability so a contract's tolerance comes from the source. *([Vitkavage, Irene and Massoud 1990](/writing/interface-study-vitkavage-1990))*
- A pull as a motion through a furnace profile: `PULL DISTANCE 54 cm DURATION t PROFILE <furnace axial temperature profile>`, so that the wafer's temperature against time follows from the paper's own words (time and distance) instead of an end temperature and a shape we invent. The paper gives distance and time; we have to write a temperature ramp. *([Deal, Sklar, Grove and Snow 1967](/writing/interface-study-deal-1967))*
- A history that ends at the measurement temperature by default (a final cooling to 25 °C written explicitly, with its gas). Our histories stop at the end of the last hot step, which is what hid the low-temperature behaviour of the charge program. *([Deal, Sklar, Grove and Snow 1967](/writing/interface-study-deal-1967))*
- A way to search a PROFILE TAU as an unknown (`VARY tau <lo>..<hi>`, or `VARY tau_factor` relative to the duration). The exponential pull had to be tried as a handful of declared variants. *([Deal, Sklar, Grove and Snow 1967](/writing/interface-study-deal-1967))*
- A tag for which samples were measured with a gold probe on bare oxide and which were metallized and given the 550 °C treatment: an optional step (`EVENT … OPTIONAL`, or two histories under one measured value), since the paper does not say which tabulated value is which. *([Deal, Sklar, Grove and Snow 1967](/writing/interface-study-deal-1967))*
- An ambient for “the end of the tube”: where the slice sits after the pull (open tube, flowing oxygen, room air) is part of the history and has no word. *([Deal, Sklar, Grove and Snow 1967](/writing/interface-study-deal-1967))*
- **Cooling with a freezing point.** With PROFILE exponential the language can now cool a wafer realistically, but the charge program then keeps moving charge down to room temperature, because its oxygen rate was fitted with an activation energy of 0.05 eV. A program needs a rate that vanishes as the wafer cools, fitted against pulls written as real cooling curves; then the pull's end temperature stops being a free number. *([Deal and Razouk 1980](/writing/interface-study-deal-razouk-1980))*
- **Doping as an input.** DOPING is recorded on each sample and read by nothing. The report's n-type and p-type wafers differ by more than the tolerance. *([Deal and Razouk 1980](/writing/interface-study-deal-razouk-1980))*
- **The anneal's gas as a separate level.** Nitrogen and argon are one curve in the report and one level in the program; if they differ (the 1100 °C rows hint that they might), the program needs a level per inert gas. *([Deal and Razouk 1980](/writing/interface-study-deal-razouk-1980))*
- **Which step is the oxidation.** The fixed-charge and trap-density programs take the oxidation temperature from the first oxygen-bearing RUN. A boat-in written as a heating ramp (`TEMP 25->1050 PROFILE exponential`) would then be read as an oxidation at 25 °C, so the boat-in here had to be written as a hold at furnace temperature. A `ROLE oxidation|anneal|load|pull` on each RUN would let programs find the step by what it is, and let a push-in be written as the heating it is. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- **An unknown that is an offset, not a duration.** “Does the printed time include the 3 min boat-in?” is one question for all 24 wafers whose oxidation times run from 1.5 to 151 min. `VARY duration` on the boat-in stands in for it; `VARY offset -180..0` on the oxidation, shared across samples, would say it directly. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- **A choice of gas as an unknown.** The ramp from 900 to 1050 °C and the withdrawal after the anneal series have unknown gases. The language varies numbers only; the gas had to become a Python variant. `VARY ambient inert_N2|dry_O2` would make it a declared unknown. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- **A wafer split in two.** In chapter 5 each wafer was cleaved and only one half had forming gas; Figure 5.9's trap density is from one half and its fixed charge from the other. `EVENT Cleave` records it, but one history cannot carry two halves. A `SPLIT` that forks the trajectory into named halves, with each observation bound to its half, would let both values be compared on the right history. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- **An etch that removes oxide.** The etched-back oxides are Hung's control: same growth, different final thickness. `EVENT EtchBack KIND etch` takes nothing off the simulated oxide. A statement that sets or removes thickness (`ETCH REMOVE 25 nm` or `ETCH TO 14.5 nm`) is needed before any program with a thickness term can be tested against this control. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- **How a charge was extracted.** Hung's Qf uses φMS = -0.715 V from the etched-back intercept. At 10 nm, 0.1 V of φMS is 2.1 × 10^11 cm⁻² of charge; at 40 nm it is 0.5 × 10^11. An observation statement carrying the φMS, the frequency and whether the half had forming gas would let charge from different laboratories be compared on one basis. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- **Gas by pressure in every program.** Writing `mix:O2=0.2,N2=0.8` now reaches the programs, but the thin-oxide growth program ignores the oxygen pressure and grows oxide in nitrogen. That is a predictor change, not a language one, and it decides every 20% and 50% thickness on this page. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- **Rounded and typical values.** Table 4.2 gives “~5×10^10” for a group of four, and chapter 5 reports “only typical or representative results”. A result's tolerance should be able to say it is a rounding of a group value, so that a search does not fit one wafer to it, as happened with the forming-gas time here. *([Hung 1987](/writing/interface-study-hung-1987))*
- A clock reference for a RUN: `TIME_ZERO at_load | at_temperature | at_gas_on` (or a signed `OFFSET <s>`), so that “time” on a figure axis can be stated as what it is. Here the offset had to be an extra 1 s step, because a RUN cannot have zero duration and VARY cannot go negative. *([Song, Dhar, Feldman, Chung and Williams 2004](/writing/interface-study-song-2004))*
- Measurements part-way through a history: `MEASURE <observable> AFTER <step>` followed by more steps, so a cumulatively oxidized sample (oxidize, unload, measure, reload, oxidize) is one history with several measured points. Today each point has to be a separate sample built by a variant function. *([Song, Dhar, Feldman, Chung and Williams 2004](/writing/interface-study-song-2004))*
- An optional or repeated step (`REPEAT <n> { … }`) for the reload of a cumulative series, with its own VARY on the per-reload time. *([Song, Dhar, Feldman, Chung and Williams 2004](/writing/interface-study-song-2004))*
- OFFCUT as a field a program reads, so that this on-axis data and Kobayashi's 4° off-axis epilayers are not the same sample to the growth program; and a word for the measurement technique (RBS or ellipsometry) on an observable. *([Song, Dhar, Feldman, Chung and Williams 2004](/writing/interface-study-song-2004))*
- A cooling rate as a statement (`COOL RATE <K/min> TO <T> [BOUND upper|lower]`), so “< 70 °C/min” is written as the paper gives it rather than as an invented end temperature and duration. The rate also needs its own furnace, so a cooling difference is not silently also a furnace difference. *([Kobayashi et al. 2017](/writing/interface-study-kobayashi-2017))*
- A furnace or equipment field on a RUN (`FURNACE resistive | rf_induction`), and the residual oxygen it is known for (under 1 ppm for one, not reported for the other). Here the two cooling rates are two furnaces. *([Kobayashi et al. 2017](/writing/interface-study-kobayashi-2017))*
- A transfer through air as a RUN-like step with its own gas and time (`TRANSFER AMBIENT air DURATION …`): the Transfer here is an EVENT, so any exposure of the interface to room air between furnaces cannot reach a program. *([Kobayashi et al. 2017](/writing/interface-study-kobayashi-2017))*
- OFFCUT read by programs (4° off-axis here, on-axis in Song 2004), and the measurement method on an observable (1 MHz high-low counts fewer states than a 100 MHz reference, the paper's Figure 4). *([Kobayashi et al. 2017](/writing/interface-study-kobayashi-2017))*
- For the predictor: a small tolerance on a state's declared bounds, or a hard clamp, so that a long low-temperature hold does not refuse a history at exactly 1.00. *([Kobayashi et al. 2017](/writing/interface-study-kobayashi-2017))*
- An isotope in a gas: `mix:18O2=0.98,16O2=0.02 PRESSURE 0.01 Torr`, so that the enrichment and the total pressure are stated and a program can read them. Today the isotope is implicit in the program and the pressure, though written, reaches nothing. *([Goncharova et al. 2011](/writing/interface-study-goncharova-2011))*
- A layer in the sample with its own composition that a program reads as an initial state (`LAYER interlayer SiOxNy THICKNESS 6 Å O:N 5:1`), so that the 6 Å oxynitride and its nitrogen start in the interface reservoir instead of being left out. *([Goncharova et al. 2011](/writing/interface-study-goncharova-2011))*
- A check in the predictor that a program's operators can act in the history's gas: a program whose source term needs oxygen should refuse, or warn, on a RUN in vacuum or argon instead of acting as if the gas were present. *([Goncharova et al. 2011](/writing/interface-study-goncharova-2011))*
- Measurement in the middle of a history (`MEASURE … AFTER Anneal10min`, then more steps): Figure 2's 10 min and +30 min are one film measured twice, which today must be two separate samples. *([Goncharova et al. 2011](/writing/interface-study-goncharova-2011))*
- Temperature in K as a unit on TEMP (`TEMP 763 K`): 763 K is written 489.85 °C, and the paper's own 763 K, 773 K and 490 °C for the same anneal are easier to keep apart when the unit is the paper's. *([Goncharova et al. 2011](/writing/interface-study-goncharova-2011))*
- **A rate that freezes.** PROFILE exponential now lets a history say how a wafer cools. This study shows the language cannot yet stop a program from moving charge at room temperature. The ontology could carry, per operator, a temperature (or activation energy) below which it is declared inactive, and the predictor could refuse a history that runs an operator outside it. That would turn the hidden 400 °C cut-off into a stated, testable property. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1982))*
- **The gas a wafer cools in.** A pull leaves one gas and cools in another (oxygen in the tube, nitrogen at the flushed mouth, air in the room). A RUN has one AMBIENT. A PROFILE that names the gas after withdrawal, or a WITHDRAW step with its own gas, would make the variant that scores best here a statement. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1982))*
- **HCl in a mixture.** “20 min 1% HCl/Ar etch” cannot be written: the mixture gases are O2, N2, H2, H2O and Ar. Adding HCl (and Cl2) would record the etch and, later, the HCl oxidations of Razouk and Deal's Figure 9. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1982))*
- **One wafer measured several times.** The cycling is one sequence of anneals with a measurement after each. Five separate histories hide that they are prefixes of one. A MEASURE event inside a history whose readings are the scored values would state it once and would show that the metal must come off between measurements. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1982))*
- **Where a starting value comes from.** The charge program's initial state is Deal's 1967 line for the oxidation temperature. Stanford's as-grown values sit below it on (111). The starting point is a laboratory property hidden in a program, and should be a stated input (for example `INITIAL Q_f FROM laboratory` with the 1967 line as one choice). *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1982))*
- **Time zero of an anneal.** Figure 5 times count from an unstated moment (the push, or reaching temperature). TIMING says whether a duration is stated, not what it is counted from. An `ORIGIN push|at_temperature|gas_switch` on a RUN would carry it. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1982))*
- **Repeat durations.** The second 25 h and 20 min of the cycling are assumed equal to the first. A `TIMING assumed_same_as <step>` would make the assumption visible. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1982](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1982))*
- **A laboratory as a property of the sample.** The largest single error here (4 to 7 times) is the laboratory. The ontology has the process factor `laboratory` but no sample or history field that records where a wafer was made and measured, so no program can carry a laboratory level, and the dataset cannot say which numbers share one. *([Razouk and Deal 1979](/writing/interface-study-razouk-deal-1979))*
- **An unknown that is a measured quantity.** The oxidation time here should be inferred from a thickness the paper states. VARY lets us search the time, but the range had to be computed by hand from the 1965 law; a statement `INFER duration FROM Thickness 120..220 nm` would let the language derive it and record that it was derived. *([Razouk and Deal 1979](/writing/interface-study-razouk-deal-1979))*
- **Halves of one wafer.** Every value here comes in pairs: one half annealed in hydrogen, one not. Two separate SAMPLEs lose that they share an oxidation; a `CLEAVE` that forks one history into two would carry it. *([Razouk and Deal 1979](/writing/interface-study-razouk-deal-1979))*
- **Cooling in an end-piece.** “Pulled … in less than 3 sec into a quartz elephant” is a fast withdrawal followed by an unknown dwell in a closed, still oxygen-filled quartz piece. A RUN with PROFILE exponential can hold the cooling but the language has no word for where the wafer is. *([Razouk and Deal 1979](/writing/interface-study-razouk-deal-1979))*
- **Mixtures with HCl and pyrogenic steam.** Figure 9's 5% and 10% HCl in oxygen cannot be written (the mixture gases are O2, N2, H2, H2O, Ar), so that figure is left off this page. *([Razouk and Deal 1979](/writing/interface-study-razouk-deal-1979))*
- **Doping read by a program.** Figure 8's n- and p-type (100) differ by 40% at 1100 and 1200 °C; DOPING is recorded on every sample and read by nothing. *([Razouk and Deal 1979](/writing/interface-study-razouk-deal-1979))*
- **The predictor:** the trap program does not respond to the gas of a step or to a pull, and labels (111) without hydrogen “outside the tested scope” while still reporting a number 35 to 48 times low. A refusal would be more honest than a number. *([Razouk and Deal 1979](/writing/interface-study-razouk-deal-1979))*
- **A starting oxide on the sample.** The 230 Å is a PARAMETER of the program and applies to every history, wet included, where the paper's own start is zero. A sample field such as `STARTING_OXIDE: 0 nm` (read by the growth programs, with the program's intercept as its default) would let wet and dry slices of one preparation differ, and would let the alignment search it. *([Deal and Grove 1965](/writing/interface-study-deal-grove-1965))*
- **Water as an oxidant.** `wet_O2` has no partial pressures; written as a mixture the water reaches no program, and the 1965 program grows the 16% oxygen share. A wet growth program (Table I constants, B with 16.3 kcal/mole) reading p_H2O is needed before any wet history means anything. *([Deal and Grove 1965](/writing/interface-study-deal-grove-1965))*
- **Pressure on B only.** The paper's law has B proportional to the oxidant pressure and A independent of it. Our operator scales the whole rate. A program that reads p_O2 only in B would be the paper's law for mixtures, which Study B (Krzeminski's 10% oxygen ramp) needs. *([Deal and Grove 1965](/writing/interface-study-deal-grove-1965))*
- **One slice measured several times.** The language cannot say that a curve's points are the same slice taken out, measured and put back (an EVENT unload, measure, reload between RUNs of one sample) or separate slices. The paper does not say which; the language should at least be able to write both. *([Deal and Grove 1965](/writing/interface-study-deal-grove-1965))*
- **A support label per gas.** The planar growth program's label claims wet and steam steps grow nothing, but a mixture makes it grow the oxygen share. The label should be computed from what the program reads (p_O2) rather than from the gas class. *([Deal and Grove 1965](/writing/interface-study-deal-grove-1965))*
- **A starting oxide a program reads.** The single most useful addition. The thin-oxide program starts every history at its fitted 1.71 nm, so Massoud's 1.0 nm wafers, Krzeminski's HF-dipped wafers and a 1.53 nm post-ramp oxide all start the same. With `STARTING_OXIDE` read by the growth programs (default: the program's fitted value), the search's other-laboratory test (start at the measured 1.53 nm) and the predictor would give one answer instead of two. *([Krzeminski et al. 2007](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2007))*
- **Growth programs that read the oxygen pressure.** The thin-oxide program has no p_O2 in its rate. It grows in nitrogen (0.2 nm in a 30 min reflow at 675 °C) and grows a 9% oxygen ramp as pure oxygen. Multiplying B (or the power law's constant) by p_O2/p_ref, as the 1965 program does, would make the stated cycle meaningful; the alignment's ramp of 580 s is a symptom. *([Krzeminski et al. 2007](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2007))*
- **Time zero as a statement.** The datasets count time from the start of the main stage; the language counts from the first RUN. A marker such as `EVENT TimeZero KIND other` that results can refer to, or a `t0` on the dataset rows, would let the stored recipe hold the whole cycle without moving every time. *([Krzeminski et al. 2007](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2007))*
- **A curve of separate wafers.** Each of the paper's points is a wafer that went through the whole cycle; Massoud's are one wafer watched in situ. The study format can sample in situ (curves within a RUN) but needs one case per wafer for the ex-situ points. The language should say which kind of series a dataset is. *([Krzeminski et al. 2007](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2007))*
- **A fast first regime.** Neither the 1965 law nor the searched power law grows the first 1.5 nm of a bare surface; both fold it into a starting thickness. An operator for it (or a second state for the first monolayers) is what Krzeminski's ramp asks for, and what its own reaction-rate model provides. *([Krzeminski et al. 2007](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2007))*
- **Exposure to air before an ex-situ measurement.** An uncaptioned figure shows 0.25–0.37 nm of growth in 90 min of air. A storage EVENT with a duration and an ambient (room air) that a program can read would carry it. *([Krzeminski et al. 2007](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2007))*
- **Growth in dry oxygen and temperature in the nanowire program.** The paper's cycle puts the wires through 750 → 850 °C and 5 min at 850 °C in pure oxygen before any steam. The radial program's rate is p_H2O × constant, so these steps grow nothing, and the missing oxide reappears as a wet time 77% longer than stated. A dry channel (rate ∝ p_O2 with its own constant) and an Arrhenius temperature dependence would let the stated cycle be simulated as stated, and would let the ramp unknowns be inferred instead of being invisible. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **A rate constant that carries the gas it was measured in.** The program's rate was measured in this furnace's pyrogenic steam, then multiplied by p_H2O/1 atm. Writing the gas truthfully as a mixture lowers the rate. A PARAMETER should be able to say “measured at p_H2O = the furnace's own” so that a stated mixture and the calibration are not counted twice; today the steam fraction and the wet time are interchangeable unknowns. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **A starting oxide on the sample.** Figure A1's bulk line extrapolates to about 9 nm at zero wet time; the wires had an HF strip then a 20 W oxygen plasma. Neither program can start a wire with an oxide shell. A sample field `OXIDE_NM`, read as the initial shell, would separate the oxide grown before time zero from the oxide grown in the stated time. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **Shape must select the program.** The predictor does not read SHAPE: a nanosheet stored with DIAMETER_NM is run as a cylinder, and a SiGe nanosheet is run by planar programs (labelled outside scope, but still numbers). `SHAPE: nanosheet` should run a flat-sidewall program (the radial program with a → ∞ gives one) or refuse. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **Gas in the SiGe growth program.** The Rabie program grows at its wet-oxidation rate in any gas, including the dry-oxygen ramp and the nitrogen steps' temperature. It should refuse, or read p_H2O and p_O2, before the furnace-cycle unknowns can be searched on SiGe. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **Furnace runs as data.** All Si structures went through one run and both SiGe compositions through another, at different times chosen per material. The alignment shares unknowns per run (`case["run"]`), but the history language has no statement for it; a `BATCH` of samples under one trajectory would put this in the history itself. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **An observable for what the paper measures.** Figure 5(a) is the increase of the outer diameter; Figure 5(b) is the core after a buffered-oxide etch. The dataset turns them into an oxide thickness, which already assumes the etch removes no silicon. Observables `Outer_diameter` and `Core_diameter_after_strip` would let the program be scored on the measured quantities and show the volume balance the data do not close. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **Faceting and sidewall orientation.** Above 60 nm the paper's Si wires are faceted by faster growth on {110}. A wire has one rate around its circumference in our language; a sidewall orientation mix on the sample would let that be tested. *([Müller, Lecestre, Demoulin, Cristiano, Hartmann and Larrieu 2023](/writing/interface-study-muller-2023))*
- **A reference sample in the same run.** The nanobeams were oxidized beside the wires; their oxide is the furnace's flat-surface rate. The language cannot say that two samples shared a furnace run, nor let a program take its rate from a measured co-processed sample. Here it had to be smuggled in as a steam fraction per case. A `BATCH` of samples under one trajectory, with a `REFERENCE` sample whose measured value is an input, would make that explicit and stop the steam fraction meaning two things. *([Krzeminski, Han and Larrieu 2012](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2012))*
- **A starting oxide on the sample.** The ~5 nm at t = 0 has no place: the radial program starts from bare silicon, and writing it as extra steam time grows it radially with the wire's slowdown. A sample field `OXIDE_NM` read as the initial shell (b > a at t = 0) would let the 5 nm be tested as native or ramp oxide. *([Krzeminski, Han and Larrieu 2012](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2012))*
- **Shapes beyond a cylinder.** Nanobeams (flat sidewalls) and nanorings (concave) are half of this paper's data and have no SHAPE a program reads. A `SHAPE: nanobeam` should select a flat-sidewall program, and a `SHAPE: nanoring` with an inner radius should select the concave sign of Eq. 1; today a beam stored with DIAMETER_NM is silently run as a cylinder. *([Krzeminski, Han and Larrieu 2012](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2012))*
- **Temperature and gas in the nanowire program.** Its rate depends on p_H2O only, so ramps, dry oxygen and the 850 °C itself are invisible. An Arrhenius rate and a dry-oxygen channel would let the furnace-cycle unknowns mean something. *([Krzeminski, Han and Larrieu 2012](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2012))*
- **Which form runs.** The predictor runs the viscous shell fitted on one paper while the project's own search selected another form on two. A program registry that records which form a search selected, and runs that one, would make the page and the search agree. *([Krzeminski, Han and Larrieu 2012](/writing/interface-study-krzeminski-2012))*
- **Wet oxygen by its steam pressure, or by its source.** `wet_O2` carries no partial pressures. A history should be able to say `mix:H2O=x,O2=1-x`, as here, or name the source (`BUBBLER 95 C`, `PYROGENIC H2:O2 1.8`) from which the pressure follows. Here the fraction moves the layer extent from 47 to 92 nm. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **Constants that belong to a condition, and a refusal outside it.** The program's k1, k2, k3 and DSiGe are the paper's for 800 °C, wet oxygen, 14%. A parameter should carry the conditions it was chosen for (`VALID T 800; AMBIENT wet; GE 0.14`), so the predictor labels or refuses a 700 °C steam history instead of answering it. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **Programs that read the gas.** The Rabie program ignores the ambient entirely: a push or a cooling in nitrogen would grow oxide in it, and dry oxidations (David 2015) are run with wet-oxygen constants. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **A starting oxide on the sample.** The model's initial oxide (“very small thickness Lox”) is a 1 nm hypothesis inside the program. The early LeGoues points ask for about 10 nm; a `STARTING_OXIDE` field would make that an unknown the alignment can search. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **Report every observable a program computes.** The Rabie program computes the germanium at the front (51.5% here) and the predictor drops it, reporting the enrichment relation's 44% under the same name. Two programs answering one target should both be reported, each with its name. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **A measurement with no time.** “A 50-nm-thick Ge-rich layer was obtained with up to 75% Ge” has no oxidation time. A result should be able to say `AT unknown` (or a range of times) and be compared over that range, not at the time we chose. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **An upper value as data.** “Up to 75%” is scored as 75 ± 10%. A result should carry `≤`, `≥` or `about`, so that a program giving 60% is not counted as wrong by the same rule as one giving 44%. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **A finite alloy layer.** The source experiments are epilayers of unstated thickness; Table VI consumes up to 425 nm of alloy. The sample cannot say how thick the alloy is or what lies under it. *([Rabie, Haddara and Carette 2005](/writing/interface-study-rabie-2005))*
- **A layered sample.** “34 nm Si0.8Ge0.2 on 12 nm Si on 10 nm BOX” is recorded as a FILM string that nothing reads. The sample needs layers with thickness and composition (`LAYER SiGe { COMPOSITION: Si0.8Ge0.2; THICKNESS: 34 nm; STRAIN: compressive }`) and programs that stop consuming a layer when it is gone. This paper's whole second half (6 h, 13 h, 14 h, 15 h) depends on it. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **Constants tied to a gas and a condition, with a refusal outside them.** The predictor answers a dry 950 °C oxidation with wet 800 °C constants and labels it “direction only”. Parameters should carry the conditions they were chosen for, and a history outside them should be labelled or refused. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **One oxide per history.** Two programs report on one SiGe history and grow oxide 16 times apart (Rabie 77.5 nm, inventory about 5 nm at 800 °C, 90 min). The predictor should take the oxide from one program and feed it to the others, or report the disagreement. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **Scope read from the oxidation, not from every step.** A ramp from room temperature puts every number “outside the tested scope”. Scope should be judged on the steps that do the work (the hold), with ramps reported separately. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **A furnace cycle as a unit.** “By steps of 30 min in accordance with the RTO technical specifications” is a repeated cycle (ramp, 30 min, ramp). A `REPEAT n { … }` block, or a tool with its own ramp law, would write it in one line instead of 90 RUNs. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **VARY on a time constant.** A cooling written as `PROFILE exponential TAU` cannot have its TAU searched; here the cooling had to be written as a straight line to make it an unknown. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **Germanium lost as GeO2.** The paper reports under 10% lost by oxidation (about 26% from its own thicknesses); the inventory conserves germanium exactly. A loss flux, or at least a declared bound on it, belongs in the inventory program. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **Strain as a sample property.** Relaxed against fully strained is the paper's subject (Eqs. 1 and 2); the language has no field for it that a program could read. *([David et al. 2015](/writing/interface-study-david-2015))*
- **A starting oxide on the sample.** The paper's two figures disagree on it (0 or 1 nm) and our program holds it as a fitted parameter. A `SAMPLE … STARTING_OXIDE <nm>` field that growth programs read would make it an unknown the alignment can search and a fact a paper can state. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
- **Growth programs that read the oxygen pressure.** The germanium program grows oxide at full rate in vacuum and at half an atmosphere. Every growth law should multiply by a pressure dependence (linear in p_O2 for the parabolic term at least); then the heat-up, the fill and the cooling in vacuum become testable instead of inert. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
- **A pressure that changes within a step.** “Oxygen was admitted” into a closed chamber at 150 sccm is a ramp of pressure, as a ramp of temperature is. `RUN … PRESSURE 0->1` (or a pressure PROFILE) would let the fill be written as stated, with the chamber volume as the unknown. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
- **A measured clock origin.** The paper's time zero is the admission of oxygen, which is the start of the fill, not of our Oxidation step. A curve should name the event its clock starts at (`CLOCK FROM Fill`), so a fill or ramp in front does not shift every point. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
- **Two observables for one oxide.** Total thickness of a two-layer optical model, the GeO2 layer alone, the interface layer (GeO2 + amorphous Ge, 1.4 to 4.8 nm), and a single-layer real-time value are four numbers for one sample here. The ontology has one Thickness. An interface-layer observable and an observation model per technique would let Table 1 be scored. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
- **Scope from the oxidation, not from the first oxygen step.** The predictor labels a history by the start temperature of its first oxygen step, so a ramp in oxygen makes a 550 °C oxidation “outside the tested scope”. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
- **A germanium clean.** The vocabulary of pre-oxidation cleans is silicon's; bromine-methanol with buffered HF cannot be named. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
- **The program as a file.** The selected germanium law is generated in memory by scripts/search_growth.py; writing it to experiments/ as the SiC ones are would let this page print the model it ran. *([Wang, Hu and Irene 1994](/writing/interface-study-wang-1994))*
